claim: Choanoflagellates are the closest living relatives of animals.

evidence: Based on established phylogenetic knowledge

claim: The S. rosetta genome has been sequenced.

claim: 16 total rosette defect mutants were classified into four broad phenotypic classes.
source: Comparing the phenotypes of the 16 total rosette defect mutants in the presence and absence of RIFs allowed us to classify four broad phenotypic classes: (1) Class A mutants that have wild type morphologies in the absence of RIFs and entirely lack rosettes in the presence of RIFs, (2) Class B mutants that have wild type morphologies in the absence of RIFs and develop reduced levels of rosettes with aberrant structures in the presence of RIFs, (3) Class C mutants that produce large clumps of cells in both the presence and absence of RIFs while forming little to no rosettes in the presence of RIFs, and (4) a Class D mutant that exist primarily as solitary cells, with no linear chains of cells detected in the absence of RIFs and no rosettes detected in the presence of RIFs (Supplementary file - Table S1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from phenotypic analysis

claim: Seafoam, Soapsuds, Jumble, and Couscous form amorphous, tightly packed clumps of cells, both in the presence and absence of RIFs, but never develop into rosettes.
source: For this study, we focused on four Class C mutants — Seafoam, Soapsuds, Jumble, and Couscous (previously named Branched in Levin et al., 2014) — that form amorphous, tightly packed clumps of cells, both in the presence and absence of RIFs, but never develop into rosettes (Table 1; Figure 1A,B).

claim: The clumps formed by Class C mutants contain a few to hundreds of mutant cells that pack together haphazardly.
source: We found that the clumps contain a few to hundreds of mutant cells that pack together haphazardly, unlike wild type rosettes in which all cells are oriented with their basal poles toward the rosette center and their apical flagella extending out from the rosette surface (Alegado et al., 2012; Levin et al., 2014; Woznica et al., 2016).

claim: In wild type rosettes, all cells are oriented with their basal poles toward the rosette center and their apical flagella extending out from the rosette surface.

claim: Wild type rosettes are structurally stable and shear resistant.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to Levin et al., 2014

claim: The cell clumps formed by Class C mutants were sensitive to shear and separated into solitary cells upon pipetting or vortexing the culture.

claim: Mutant cells re-aggregated into new clumps within minutes following exposure to shear.

claim: Wild type cells never formed clumps following exposure to shear.

claim: The speed of clump reformation (less than the ~6 hr required for a single cell division) demonstrates that cell aggregation alone is sufficient to drive clump formation.
source: Both the speed of clump reformation (less than the ~6 hr required for a single cell division (Levin et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and the observation of cell clumping in the absence of cell division (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) demonstrate that cell aggregation alone is sufficient to drive clump formation.

claim: The observation of cell clumping in the absence of cell division demonstrates that cell aggregation alone is sufficient to drive clump formation.

claim: Each of the mutants tested displayed a mild defect in cell proliferation.

claim: Clumps formed in both the presence and absence of RIFs were comparable in size for Jumble and Couscous.

claim: Cell aggregation was not strain-specific, as unlabeled Jumble and Couscous mutant cells adhered to wild type cells identified by their expression of cytoplasmic mWasabi.

claim: The Rosetteless mutant was crossed to a phenotypically wild type Mapping Strain and relied on genotyping of haploid F1s at 60 PCR-verified genetic markers.

(2014) study, the Rosetteless mutant was crossed to a phenotypically wild type Mapping Strain (previously called Isolate B in Levin et al., 2014) and relied on genotyping of haploid F1s at 60 PCR-verified genetic markers that differed between the Rosetteless mutant and the Mapping Strain (Levin et al., 2014).

claim: The low level of sequence polymorphism among S. rosetta laboratory strains and abundance of repetitive sequences in the draft genome assembly made it difficult to identify and validate additional genetic markers.
source: Compounding the problem, the low level of sequence polymorphism among S. rosetta laboratory strains and abundance of repetitive sequences in the draft genome assembly (Fairclough et al., 2013; Levin et al., 2014) made it difficult to identify and validate additional genetic markers, while genotyping at individual markers proved labor intensive and costly.
evidence: Based on the challenges encountered and supported by citations

claim: Bulk segregation methods developed in other systems were modified for use in S. rosetta.

claim: A bulk segregant approach successfully pinpointed the causal mutation for Rosetteless.

evidence: Supported by experimental data validating the bulk segregant approach

evidence: Supported by experimental data from mapping crosses

claim: The diploid cells each secreted a flask-shaped attachment structure called a theca and were obligately unicellular.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Five sequence variants in Jumble segregated with both the clumping and rosette defects using the bulk segregant approach.

claim: In a backcross of mutant F1 progeny to the Mapping Strain, the tight linkage of the SNV to the rosette defect phenotype was confirmed.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: All F2 progeny that displayed a rosette defect also had a clumping phenotype.
source: Moreover, all F2 progeny that displayed a rosette defect also had a clumping phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from backcross analysis

claim: The single point mutation at genome position 1:1,919,681 causes both the clumping and rosette defect phenotypes in Jumble mutants.
source: Given the tight linkage of both traits with the SNV and the absence of any detectable neighboring sequence variants, we infer that the single point mutation at genome position 1:1,919,681 causes both the clumping and rosette defect phenotypes in Jumble mutants.
evidence: Inferred from tight linkage and absence of other variants

claim: The mutant jumble gene has a T to C mutation at nucleotide 1109 that causes an amino acid substitution of proline to leucine at amino acid position 305.
